title: Adrenal (Addisonian) Crisis
scenario: A 44-year-old female with a known history of Addison's disease presents to the emergency department with 2 days of severe nausea, vomiting, and progressive weakness after stopping her hydrocortisone during a flu-like illness.

lines: 44-year-old female brought in by partner for 2 days of intractable vomiting, diffuse abdominal pain, and profound fatigue. States she ran out of her steroid pills during a viral illness last week and did not refill them. Skin appears hyperpigmented at knuckles and oral mucosa. Lethargic but arousable, oriented x3. Reports dizziness on standing.
Two large-bore IV lines established. Blood drawn for labs, cortisol, and cultures. Placed supine with legs elevated. Cardiac monitor and continuous pulse oximetry applied.
IV hydrocortisone 100 mg administered per order. Rapid infusion of 0.9% normal saline with dextrose in progress. Repeat point-of-care glucose obtained.
Client reports nausea resolving and feeling stronger. Skin warm, no longer diaphoretic. Voided 250 mL clear urine. Mentation clearer, sitting up in bed.
Hydrocortisone 20 mg PO every morning, 10 mg PO every afternoon (home dose, not taken x 5 days)
Administer hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus now, then 50 mg IV every 6 hours
Infuse 0.9% normal saline with 5% dextrose, 1 L over first hour
Recheck sodium, potassium, and glucose in 2 hours
Notify provider for SBP < 90 mmHg or potassium > 6.0 mEq/L

children.subject: Medical-Surgical

options.text: Intractable vomiting with dizziness on standing
Lethargy that is arousable and oriented x3

children.rationale: Hypotension, volume depletion from vomiting, and altered mentation signal circulatory collapse in adrenal crisis; hyperpigmentation points to chronic Addison's disease. Near-normal oxygenation and a low-grade temp are less urgent.

children.subject: Medical-Surgical
children.stem: For each finding, click to specify whether it reflects cortisol deficiency, aldosterone deficiency, or both. Each finding may reflect more than one.
children.rationale: Cortisol loss impairs gluconeogenesis and vascular tone (hypoglycemia, hypotension). Aldosterone loss causes sodium wasting and potassium retention (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia). Sodium and BP are affected by both hormones.

children.subject: Medical-Surgical
children.stem: Complete the sentence. The nurse determines that the priority problem is {1} and the priority collaborative intervention is {2}.
children.rationale: The immediate life threat is circulatory collapse from cortisol and volume deficiency. IV glucocorticoid replacement plus saline resuscitation reverses the crisis; potassium supplementation would be dangerous given existing hyperkalemia.

children.subject: Medical-Surgical
children.stem: For each intervention, click to specify whether it is indicated or contraindicated for this client.

rows.text: Monitor cardiac rhythm for peaked T waves

children.rationale: Glucocorticoid replacement, saline with dextrose, and cardiac monitoring for hyperkalemia are all indicated. Giving potassium or restricting sodium would worsen the hyperkalemia and hyponatremia of adrenal crisis.

children.subject: Medical-Surgical
children.stem: After starting IV hydrocortisone and fluid resuscitation, which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor blood pressure closely for response
Withhold all further fluids until output improves
Encourage the client to ambulate to the bathroom

children.rationale: Ongoing monitoring of glucose, electrolytes, blood pressure, and cardiac rhythm tracks the response to steroids and fluids. Withholding fluids or ambulating a hypotensive client would be unsafe.

children.subject: Medical-Surgical
children.stem: Which findings indicate the treatment has been effective? Select all that apply.

options.text: Nausea resolving and client feeling stronger

children.rationale: Rising blood pressure, slowing heart rate, resolving nausea, and improved mentation show the crisis is reversing. Continued hypotension would indicate ongoing shock, not improvement.
